explainBack.question: Why can Cursor Projects keep working on my page after I close my laptop, yet still need my own computer for testing?
explainBack.answer: Because the Project runs on its own computer in the cloud, the work does not depend on your laptop being open; the coordinator plans and delegates coding to other agents there. But testing that depends on your machine's environment cannot happen in the cloud, so Cursor says the coordinator starts a separate local agent on your computer, and the finished result comes back to you to check.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P003 states the cloud computer keeps the job running when the laptop closes and that a local agent is started when testing is needed on your machine; P002 establishes the coordinator's plan-and-delegate role.
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; nothing had to be imported from outside the text.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A freelancer uses Projects to build a client's portfolio site with a booking form that must be tested against a database running only on her own machine, and she wants edits to continue overnight while her laptop is shut.
unseenTransfer.question: Which parts of her job continue after she closes her laptop, and what must she still do herself?
unseenTransfer.answer: Page-building and copy edits can continue because the Project runs on a cloud computer independent of her laptop. The booking-form test against her local database is the separate handoff: per the article, the coordinator starts a local agent on her machine, which requires that machine to be available. When results return she must verify the form does what she asked, the links work, and nothing else on the site changed — Cursor's announcement describes the design, not a guarantee of a correct result.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P003 (cloud continuation and local-agent handoff), P004 (the stay-online vs needs-my-computer decision test), P006 (the concrete review job that remains hers).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this new scenario cleanly, confirming the explanation transfers beyond the printed example.

learningDisposition.rationale: One present defect: the artifact narrows the reader job to personal websites/apps and omits the larger-work-project half the source explicitly supports (features, migrations, months of context). A one-to-two sentence extension of the same mechanism to bigger coordinated work would repair it; all other outcomes and families are sound.

reader.summary: A clear, well-mechanized, honestly attributed news notice: the coordinator, cloud continuation, local-testing handoff, beta rollout, and the reader's remaining review job are all explained plainly with a genuinely useful decision test. Its one real defect is scope: it serves only the personal website/app reader and never extends the same mechanism to the larger work projects the source and the reader job both name.

launch.reason: The September 10 beta launch matches the source's publication and 'launching Projects' language, but 'for people building a personal website or app' is the article's audience framing; the source scopes Projects to 'larger bodies of work, such as a feature, a migration, or a full app', which is broader than stated.

coordinator.reason: Source states the coordinator agent doesn't write code itself, plans the work, delegates to implementing agents, and brings finished work back for checking; the article preserves this with 'Cursor says' attribution.

cloud-local.reason: Source: 'A Project runs on its own computer in the cloud, so closing your laptop doesn't stop it' and the coordinator 'spins up a local agent' for machine testing; the article restates both accurately with attribution and keeps the review step.

context.reason: Source describes each Project maintaining a set of files syncing across machines where agents add research, artifacts and learned instructions; 'keeps the files and notes for one longer job' is an accurate plain simplification.

beta.reason: Source states verbatim that 'Projects are available in beta and rolling out to all users starting today', matching the article's claim exactly.

factualIntegrity.reason: All material claims trace to the supplied changelog with vendor attribution retained; no contradiction exists, though the launch-audience framing is a qualification rather than a sourced fact.

freshnessReviewability.reason: Launch date (September 10), beta status, source access date and a checkable primary URL make every time-sensitive claim reviewable.

datedChange.reason: This is a single newly reported launch; nothing old is conflated with the September 10 announcement.

consequenceAndUncertainty.reason: Consequences are concrete (work continuing, local handoff, review job) and uncertainty survives: results 'come back to you to check' keeps the source's limit that the announcement proves design, not output quality.

learningDisposition.rationale: One qualified claim: the personal-website/app audience framing exceeds the source's stated scope of features, migrations and full apps. The repair is small — attribute the broader scope to Cursor or mark the personal-site case as the article's chosen example; all other claims are directly supported.

facts.summary: Four of five claims are directly supported by the Cursor changelog with correct attribution and preserved limits; the launch claim is qualified because the source describes larger bodies of work (features, migrations, full apps) rather than a personal-website audience. Dates, beta status and reviewability are all sound.
